families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai, Turkana, Samburu, Teso), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin, Pokot), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Borana/Oromo, Rendille, and Daasanach (Dhaasanac).

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based national & official lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest mother-tongue community in the central highlands (Kiambu/Kabeti, Murang'a/Metumi/Fort Hall, and Nyeri/Gaki around Mount Kenya [Kĩrĩnyaga / Kĩreĩra]); documented in Höhnel (1894), Hémery (1903), Hinde (1904), McGregor (1904), W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa'), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes of the Lake Victoria basin; documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902), Northcote (1907), Roscoe/Willis (1915), Mill-Hill Fathers (1920), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Nandi, Kipsigis/Lumbwa [Il Kakesan], Tugen/Kamasia [Kapteberewa & Nderois], Marakwet & Endo/Ndo [Chebleng], Keiyo/Elgeyo, Kabkamat/Olmo, Sangwirr, Uasin Gishu Moiven/Muttia/Il-Mokwan/I-Sirikwa, Sabaot); documented in Hollis (1909), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), BFBS (1921), Diercks & Rao (2019), Landman (2019), and Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono (2024).

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ Western Bantu dialects including Wanga (Luhanga of Buhanga), Bukusu/Masaba, Kabras, Nyala, Marama, Tsotso, Tiriki, Idakho, Isukha, and Maragoli (Logoori); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902, 1919), Purvis (1907, 1909), Roscoe (1915), Rev. N. Stam (1929 'The Bahanga', Catholic Anthropological Conference Vol. I, No. 4, pp. 143–179 — audited 100% line-by-line across the p. 145 Map, 11-generation Bakhitsetse royal genealogy from Kwandedi & Wanga to Mumia, Osundwa II & Rapando, royal sitting burial & Matungo bone procession, Fig. 1 commoner burial diagram, Fig. 2 kraal sacrificial stones & khatsu khe misango diagram, reversive -ula, 5 special sacrifices, khyembekho rainmaking, Nasayi/Were prayers & Chameleon myth, 6 practitioners, 2 ordeals, 10 omens, Makokha adoption, amakhwana twin rites, okhutekherana marriage, musiro totems & okhukhyebwa circumcision), and Payne, Pacchiarotti & Bosire eds. (2016).

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Central Bantu language of Eastern Kenya across 4 regional divisions (Ulu/Yulu [kīkamba kīluŋgalu & Kīluŋgu], East Ukamba/Kitui [aþaisu / kīþaisu], Kīkumbuliu & Mumonī, plus Anoka on Mt. Noka and the 1836 Rabai diaspora); documented in Krapf (1850), Last (1885), Hinde (1904), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Gerhard Lindblom (1920 'The Akamba in British East Africa: An Ethnological Monograph', 2nd Ed., Enlarged, Archives d'Études Orientales Vol. 17, Uppsala, pp. I–XII, 1–607, Figs. 1–167 — audited 100% line-by-line across all 35 chapters, Addenda, 7 informants, 25+ mbaī clans & brands [Figs. 17–51], 3 nžaīko initiations, musaī sticks [Figs. 1–8] & sand drawings [Figs. 9–16], nðonī & 11 kwiūa pairs, 7 women's words, kinship table, 5 atumīa meat-sharing grades, nsīlī law, kīþītū [Fig. 52] & ndundu oaths, 6 ordeals, kīŋgolə, 3 war divisions & mutīætumo honours, aīmu, īþæmbo & Muluŋgu/Mumbī/Mwatwaŋgagī prayers, kuausīa divination, unīka/mwītano arch, 17 ŋgondu substances, 45+ medicinal plants, 9 famines, 3 11-month calendars, kuseuβīa maīo teeth-chipping & bone false teeth, 11 musical instruments, kīūīśī board game, 13-part hut plan [Fig. 125], 7 traps, 28 livestock terms, mwatu beekeeping, munīo S-link chains & 3 color roots), BFBS (1921), and Jones & Freyer (2019).

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language of North Eastern Kenya; documented in Cust (1883), de Larajasse (1897), Kirk (1903, 1905), BFBS (1921), Nilsson (2016), Kimper et al. (2019), and Nurse (2019).

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Eastern Lake Victoria Bantu language of the Kisii Highlands; documented in Hobley (1902) and Johnston (1902, 1919).

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya & Tana valley Bantu cluster (Imenti, Tigania, Igembe, Mwimbi, Chuka, and Kĩtharaka); documented in Hobley (1910), Champion (1912), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Kithaka wa Mberia (2004).

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic, across 4 Clans ['L-Aiser, Il-Meñgana, Il-Mokesen, Il-Molelyan], 2 Moieties ['L-oodo-kishu & 'L-oorook-kishu], 19 Sub-Families [Il-gilat], and 5 Districts [Il-Kaputiei, En-aiposha, 'L-Oitai, Il-Kisonko, 'L-Uasinkishu], plus Laikipiak, Segellai, and Tigirri); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883), Höhnel (1894), Hildegarde Hinde (1901 'The Masai Language: Grammatical Notes Together with a Vocabulary' — audited 100% line-by-line across pp. i–xii, 1–75 [PDF pp. 1–98]: Preface critiquing Ehrhardt 1857 & Johnston, Errata slip, Rules §§ 1–23, 9 Regular Plural Suffix Methods, Sexagesimal Base-60 Counting [īp = 60], 65 Verb Conjugation Paradigms, 340 Conversational Phrases, Salutations, 3 Songs, 3 Ethnonyms, 8 Kenyan Toponyms, 10 Curses & ~1,050-entry Vocabulary with 5 Footnotes), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis & Sir Charles Eliot (1905 'The Masai: Their Language and Folklore' — audited 100% line-by-line across Parts I–VI, pp. i–xxviii, 1–359, Frontispiece & Plates I–XXVII), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, Appendix II pp. 344–349 & Plate CXXXVI), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Ateker branch: 16 principal tribes and 19 Ngoitunya & Ngolio attegir clans); documented in Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), and Barton (1921).

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya southeastern slopes (Embu & Mbeere); documented in Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Hobley (1922).

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills Bantu (Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau); documented in Shaw (1885), Taylor (1891), Wray (1894), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language of Kenya (including Kiamu, Kimvita, Kitikuu/Bajuni, Kipate, Kingozi, and Kiunguja); documented in Krapf (1850, 1882), Bishop Edward Steere (1870 'Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar', Bell & Daldy London, pp. i–xvi, 1–504 [PDF pp. 1–529] — audited 100% line-by-line across J. F. Campbell's Aug. 1, 1870 provenance & Kalila and Dimna marginalia, 6 named informants, 3 Mombasa Preface poems, 18 prose tales incl. Kimvita 'Kititi, na Fisi, na Simba' & 'Hadithi ya Liongo', all 20 verbatim Mifano, all 14 Vitendawili, 'Mashairi ya Liongo', 'Utumbuizo wa Gungu', 'Mwanzo wa Utenzi wa Ayubu', all 37 Italicized Words, all 103 Notes & all 12 Corrigenda), Bishop Edward Steere & A. C. Madan (1894 'A Handbook of the Swahili Language, as Spoken at Zanzibar', 4th Ed., SPCK London, pp. i–xxii, 1–458 [PDF pp. 1–488] — audited 100% line-by-line across U of Toronto copy PL 8702 S724 1894, Advertisements & Preface, Part I Grammar & Categorized Vocabularies pp. 1–235, 9-Language Bantu Prefix Tables pp. 234–235, Part II Vocabulary pp. 245–421 incl. all 18 Named Parts of a Kanzu p. 299 & all 41 Named Mita of Zanzibar Town pp. 346–347, and Appendices I–V pp. 425–458; plus 1918), Taylor (1891), Bateman (1901), A. C. Madan (1903 'Swahili-English Dictionary', Clarendon Press Oxford, pp. i–xix, 1–442 [PDF pp. 1–478] — audited 100% line-by-line across UC Berkeley copy PL 8703 / M33 / 1903 / MAIN, July 1903 Preface ['Bantize rather than Arabize' & asterisk (*) non-Bantu loanword system], Introduction & 8 Principal Verb-Stem Forms [incl. 6 Causal & 5 Reciprocal varieties] pp. ix–xiii, Conspectus II of 8 Noun Declensions D 1–D 8 pp. xvi–xvii, Abbreviations pp. xviii–xix, Dictionary Sections A–M Part 1 pp. 1–238 [incl. 29 gift/bribe/fee terms under *Bakshishi, 11 sticks under Bakora, 6 gun types under *Bunduki, 11 dhows under Chombo, 10 dhow ropes & 6 fibres under Kamba, Kasimele first-press coconut cream, Keke bow-drill, 6 ordeal types under Kiapo, Kiko water-pipe, April 15, 1872 Zanzibar hurricane Kimbunga, Kitanda cha mfumi loom, 19 English loans under Manowari, 18 perfumes under Manukato, Mlango carved doors, 8 palm species under Mnazi, and 65+ embedded proverbs & riddles], Closing Page of Section Z p. 442 & Clarendon Press Catalogue pp. 1–8; plus 1902, 1905, 1917), Mrs. F. Burt & Rev. W. E. Taylor (1910 'Swahili Grammar and Vocabulary', SPCK London, pp. 1–252 [PDF pp. 1–260] — audited 100% line-by-line across UCSB copy X-30323, 1910 Preface by A. E. B., Rev. W. E. Taylor's Part I Dialect Tables I–IV pp. 7–10, Phonetic Exercises 1–21 pp. 11–21 & Syllabary pp. 22–23, Part II Studies I–XXI & Grammar Tables pp. 24–131, Complete Exercise Keys pp. 132–151, Money/Weights/Measures pp. 152–153, 3 Mombasa Letters of Rabiu l-Awwal 1324 A.H. pp. 154–156, Calendar & Monsoons pp. 157–158, 14 Synonym Groups pp. 158–159, All 44 Homonym Groups pp. 159–161, and Part III A–Z Vocabulary pp. 162–252), Stigand (1915), Beech (1918), Werner (1918, 1919, 1933), Mwamzandi (2022), and Goldsmith & Mpiranya (2022).

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine coastal Sabaki sub-groups (Giriama, Digo, Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma); documented in Krapf (1850), Krapf & Rebmann (1887), Taylor (1891), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Nicolle (2016).

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language (Borana, Gabbra, Sakuye, and Tana River Orma/Bararetta); documented in Krapf (1840, 1842, 1850), Tutschek (1844–1845), Cust (1883), Foot (1913), Werner (1915), BFBS (1921), and Griefenow-Mewis (1996).

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Omo-Tana East Cushitic camel-herding pastoralists of the Kaisut and Chalbi plains (including the historical Naroshon section on the Sogota–Lomello plains); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), Fleming (1964), and Heine (1976).

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Eastern Nilotic (Ateker) language spoken in Busia County and eastern Uganda; documented in Hobley (1902), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Kitching (1915), Roscoe (1915), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River Sabaki Bantu language across 13 Upper and Lower Pokomo vyeti; documented in Krapf (1850), Würtz (1895), Werner (1913, 1915, 1933), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Mikael Samson & Darroch (1944).

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Northern Maa (Plains Nilotic) pastoralists (including historical Il Doigio, Lorogishu / Kwakituk on Angata e-'m-barta, and Lobbeyok sections); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Hobley (1910).

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo Maa-speaking irrigation farmers and fishermen (Njamus / Nyarusi across Njemps Kubwa [Liabori], Njemps Ndogo [Lekepir], and Korvan, comprising 16 clans from 6 tribes); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Beech (1911).

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch, historically Suk / Bawgott across 11 geographical divisions and 24 orten clans); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), and Barton (1921).

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) around Taveta and Lake Jipe; documented in Höhnel (1894), Steggall (1892–1906), Hollis (1910–1911), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Daasanach (Dhaasanac)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic (Western Omo-Tana) agropastoral and fishing community around Ileret on the northeastern shore of Lake Turkana; documented in Höhnel (1894 as Reshiat), Sasse (1974, 1976), Tosco (2001), Nishiguchi (2004), and Blažek (2011).

officialLanguages.notes: Used in government, courts, parliament, and education (from Grade 4 onwards).
Lingua franca spoken by over 90% of Kenyans as a first or second language.
Promoted alongside Braille and other communication formats.
